# Introduction {#sec-intro}

## Background & Motivation

Pancreatic cancer has a poor prognosis, and few patients survive five years after diagnosis [@SEER2026]. Most cases are pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). Expression studies have divided PDAC into molecular subtypes that differ in survival and in response to treatment [@Collisson2011], but the taxonomies do not agree: @Collisson2011 described three subtypes and @Bailey2016 described four. Bulk tumor samples also mix malignant and stromal cells. @Moffitt2015 used virtual microdissection to separate basal-like and classical tumor expression from normal and activated stromal expression, and in The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) cohort several subtype assignments were associated with tumor purity [@Raphael2017]. A gene expression program describes this variation in a different way. It is a set of genes that vary together across samples, and each patient has a continuous score for how strongly the program is expressed [@Brunet2004; @Kotliar2019]. Programs can capture variation within a subtype and across the tumor and stromal compartments, so they can be used to ask which molecular patterns are associated with survival.

Prognostic programs are usually found in two steps. A factorization approximates the $n\times p$ expression matrix $\mathbf{Y}$ as $\mathbf{L}\mathbf{F}^\top$, where $\mathbf{L}$ holds patient scores and $\mathbf{F}$ holds gene loadings. The estimated scores then enter a Cox proportional hazards model [@Cox1972], often with a penalty when there are many of them [@Simon2011]. This pipeline has two weaknesses. First, the factorization is fitted to explain expression, and survival plays no part in deciding which programs it finds. Variation in cell composition can dominate the fit. In the PDAC analysis of @Young2026, exocrine content was prominent in expression but contributed little to the survival model. A program that predicts survival but explains little expression variance can therefore be missed or merged into another factor. Second, the Cox model treats the estimated scores as covariates measured without error. The resulting bias in the coefficients depends on the structure of the score error [@Prentice1982; @Carroll2006], and standard errors from the second step leave out the uncertainty from estimating the programs. Supervised dimension reduction, such as screening genes by their survival association before principal components analysis [@Bair2004] or partial least squares for Cox regression [@Nygard2008], links the reduction to the outcome. It does not give posterior uncertainty for the programs or for their survival associations.

Two lines of work address parts of this problem. DeSurv adds a Cox loss to non-negative matrix factorization, so survival can influence the programs it finds, and it was evaluated in five independent PDAC cohorts [@Young2026]. Its survival coefficients are penalized point estimates, and its rank and supervision strength are tuned by cross-validated concordance outside the model. A second line of work models uncertainty in the programs. Empirical Bayes matrix factorization (EBMF) estimates a separate prior for each factor's scores and loadings [@Wang2021; @Willwerscheid2025], so the amount of shrinkage and sparsity adapts to each program. It is fitted by variational inference [@Wang2021; @Blei2017] and uses the molecular data alone. Bayesian factor models guided by an outcome exist, but they model continuous, binary, ordinal or categorical responses rather than censored survival times [@Samorodnitsky2024; @Gygi2024]. Integration methods such as iCluster [@Shen2009] and Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (MOFA) [@Argelaguet2018] model several data types together. MOFA shares patient scores across data types and gives each type its own loadings, a structure that suits matched expression and DNA methylation, but survival does not guide its factorization.

We found no empirical Bayes factorization that estimates several programs together with their Cox associations and reports posterior uncertainty for those associations. We also found none that extends such a model to matched expression and methylation with a separate loading prior for each data type. A joint model raises one more question that the two-step pipeline avoids: how much weight survival should receive relative to the molecular data. If survival receives too little weight, a joint fit finds the same programs as an expression-only fit and addresses only the second weakness. This chapter asks whether a joint Bayesian model can find prognostic programs that an expression-only factorization misses. In such a model, survival enters through its likelihood with a weight chosen from the data, and uncertainty in the programs carries into their survival associations.

## Aims & Contributions

The project has four aims. The first is to develop survival-supervised Bayesian matrix factorization (SSBMF), which jointly fits an empirical Bayes factorization of molecular data and a Cox model. Its purpose is to identify molecular programs associated with survival and to estimate those associations with posterior uncertainty. The second is to choose the strength of supervision and the number of programs from the data, so that survival shapes the programs when the survival signal supports it. The third is to extend the model to several matched data types, starting with gene expression and DNA methylation, with a separate loading prior for each type. The fourth is to evaluate the method in simulation and in independent PDAC cohorts, against two-step pipelines and existing supervised methods, and to release it as software.

This chapter presents the single-modality model and its evaluation. In SSBMF each patient's risk score projects their expression onto the program loadings, so a new patient's risk is computed from measured expression without first estimating their program scores. A survival weight $w_S$ sets how much the Cox partial likelihood counts relative to the expression likelihood in the variational objective. We derive a coordinate-ascent variational algorithm whose coefficient update accounts for posterior uncertainty in the loadings, and we check each update against a direct evaluation of the objective. We also derive the survival share, a measure of how much survival informs each loading. It grows with the survival weight and the number of events and falls with the number of genes and the program's share of expression variance, so supervision acts mainly on low-variance programs. We implement a rule that chooses $w_S$ by cross-validated partial likelihood and evaluate it in simulation and on the training data. Simulation studies examine recovery of a low-variance prognostic program, false activity under permuted survival, calibration of the risk score in validation data and convergence. On PDAC, the model is configured by cross-validation in two training cohorts and evaluated once in five external PDAC validation cohorts that were not used to choose the survival weight. It is compared with a rank-matched two-step fit, unsupervised fits of larger rank, DeSurv, an elastic-net Cox model and the PurIST subtype classifier [@Rashid2020]. Risk groups and the main prognostic programs are defined on the training data, and the genes of those programs are compared with published subtype signatures.

Continuing work completes the remaining aims. The main open problem is a survival weight that lets survival change the loadings where the data support it. We will fit the extension to expression and methylation, which shares patient scores across data types and gives each its own loading prior, and validate it in an external cohort. Rank selection under the supervised objective, a comparison with a parameterization that places the latent scores in the Cox model, and an R package complete the project.

The rest of the chapter is organized as follows. @sec-methods defines the model, the survival weight, the variational algorithm, the rule for choosing the weight and prediction in new cohorts. It then describes the simulation studies, the PDAC data, the training-only tuning protocol, the choice of gene screen, input scaling and rank, and the sensitivity analyses for the priors. The proposed extension to several data types and the comparators, risk-group rule and program classification follow. @sec-results reports the simulations, cross-validation in the training cohorts, external validation, the comparison with other prognostic models and the fitted programs. @sec-discussion interprets the loading and coefficient estimates, states the limitations and describes the continuing work.

# Methods {#sec-methods}

## Model {#sec-model}

For $n$ patients and $p$ genes, let $\mathbf{Y}$ ($n\times p$) hold log-scale expression standardized within each cohort. The expression model is
$$
\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{L}\mathbf{F}^\top + \mathbf{E},\qquad E_{ij}\sim N(0,\tau_j^{-1}),
$$
where $\mathbf{L}$ ($n\times K$) holds patient scores on $K$ programs, $\mathbf{F}$ ($p\times K$) holds gene loadings, and $\tau_j$ is the noise precision of gene $j$. Survival follows a Cox proportional hazards model [@Cox1972; @Cox1975] with Breslow handling of ties [@Breslow1974] and linear predictor
$$
\eta_i=\sum_{k=1}^K z_{ik}\beta_k,\qquad \mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{Y}\mathbf{F} .
$$
Here $z_{ik}$ is patient $i$'s expression projected onto program $k$'s loadings, and $\beta_k$ is the log hazard ratio per unit of that score. We call this the YFB parameterization, after $\boldsymbol{\eta}=(\mathbf{Y}\mathbf{F})\boldsymbol{\beta}$. The alternative, $\boldsymbol{\eta}=\mathbf{L}\boldsymbol{\beta}$, puts the latent scores in the Cox model, so a new patient's risk needs their scores to be estimated first. A comparison of the two is proposed work (@sec-comparators).

Every entry of $\mathbf{L}$ and of $\mathbf{F}$ has a point-Laplace prior, a mixture of a point mass at zero and a Laplace distribution, with its mixing proportion and scale estimated by empirical Bayes for each program [@Willwerscheid2025]. The prior lets a loading be exactly zero and lets a whole program shrink to zero. Each coefficient has a Normal prior $\beta_k\sim N(0,\sigma_k^2)$ with $\sigma_k^2$ estimated. Sensitivity analyses with other priors are described in @sec-model-checks. $\mathbf{Z}$ has no prior of its own: it is a fixed function of the observed $\mathbf{Y}$ and the loadings, so its posterior moments follow from those of $\mathbf{F}$. The objective combines the expression likelihood and the Cox partial likelihood conditional on $\mathbf{Y}$.

## Survival Weight and Objective {#sec-weight}

The model is fitted by maximizing an evidence lower bound (ELBO) over a factorized posterior $q=\prod_k q(\mathbf{l}_k)\,q(\mathbf{f}_k)\,q(\beta_k)$, the priors and $\boldsymbol{\tau}$:
$$
\mathcal F = E_q\log p(\mathbf{Y}\mid \mathbf{L},\mathbf{F},\boldsymbol{\tau}) + w_S\,E_q\,\ell_{\mathrm{Cox}}(\mathbf{Y}\mathbf{F}\boldsymbol{\beta}) - \sum_k\left[\mathrm{KL}(q_{\mathbf{l}_k}\Vert g_{\mathbf{l}_k}) + \mathrm{KL}(q_{\mathbf{f}_k}\Vert g_{\mathbf{f}_k}) + \mathrm{KL}(q_{\beta_k}\Vert g_{\beta_k})\right].
$$
The survival term has unit weight at $w_S=1$. More generally the objective is a variational bound for an update that raises the Cox partial likelihood to the power $w_S$ [@Bissiri2016; @HolmesWalker2017]. The same $w_S$ enters every update that involves survival and the monitored objective.

Rescaling a program's scores, loadings and coefficient together leaves the likelihood unchanged. After each sweep, each nonzero program is rescaled so that its posterior mean projection $\mathbf{Y} E[\mathbf{f}_k]$ has standard deviation 1 in the training data. This fixes the units of $\beta_k$ (log hazard ratio per standard deviation of the program score) and makes one value of $w_S$ mean the same thing for every program. At $w_S=0$ survival drops out of every update, including that of $\boldsymbol{\beta}$, so the fitted coefficients are zero. The unsupervised comparator is built from that fit: we take its loadings and fit a separate Cox model to the training scores $\mathbf{Y} E[\mathbf{F}]$. We call this the two-step fit. Both arms use the same rank and preprocessing. The comparison captures the combined effect of including survival in the loading update and estimating the Cox coefficients jointly under a Normal shrinkage prior.

Survival enters the factorization through the loading update. The Cox term contributes to both the precision and the linear term of that update. We use the fraction of loading precision due to the Cox term, called the survival share, to compare the relative information in the two likelihoods. The derivation shows that it grows with $w_S$, with the squared coefficient and with the number of events, and falls roughly as $1/p^2$ for a program of fixed variance share and as the square of that variance share. Survival therefore has the most influence on low-variance programs, which are the ones supervision is meant to find, and almost none on dominant programs.

## Variational Inference {#sec-vi}

The Cox partial log-likelihood is not conjugate to any prior. At each sweep it is replaced by a second-order expansion around the current linear predictor, keeping the diagonal of the Hessian, so that each update has the form of a normal-means problem solved with the ebnm package [@Willwerscheid2025]. Taking expectations under $q$, the expansion contributes the variance of $\eta_i$ as well as its mean. The coefficient update uses the posterior second moment of each score, $E[z_{ik}^2]=\bar z_{ik}^2+\sum_j y_{ij}^2\operatorname{Var}(f_{jk})$, rather than its plug-in square. The second term propagates loading uncertainty into the variational coefficient update. The loading update has an expression part and a survival part. The survival part adds $w_S$ times the Cox curvature to each loading's precision, and genes are updated one at a time so that each sees the scores refreshed by the genes before it.

One sweep updates the Taylor expansion, then for each program the coefficient, the scores $\mathbf{l}_k$ and the loadings $\mathbf{f}_k$, then the noise precisions, and then rescales the programs. Scores and loadings start from a truncated singular value decomposition. Fitting stops when the relative change in the ELBO falls below $10^{-5}$, or after 300 sweeps. The full derivation, the update schedule and a one-page algorithm are in the project derivation document. A separate script checks each update against a brute-force evaluation of the expected objective and against the code (73 checks).

A nonempty program is called survival-active when its coefficient has positive posterior SD and $|E\beta_k|/\mathrm{SD}(\beta_k)\ge1.96$. In simulation, recovery requires an absolute loading correlation of at least 0.7, an active coefficient and the correct coefficient sign after aligning the loadings. A survival-active program that matches no planted prognostic program counts as false-active. A count of false-active programs does not say how much they affect the risk score. We therefore also report their share of the variance of the risk score and their standardized coefficients.

## Choosing the Survival Weight {#sec-choose-weight}

The real-data comparison uses $w_S=1$, which performed best in the first simulation study and was retained after five-fold cross-validation on the PDAC training data (@sec-res-cv). That choice keeps the coefficient update at its Bayesian weight, but it leaves the survival share on real data very small (@sec-res-cv). A larger fixed weight is not a solution, since fixed weights of 40 or more did not converge with 2,000 genes in simulation (@sec-res-sim).

We have tested one way of setting the weight from the data. In a variant of the objective, $w_S$ multiplies both the Cox term and $\mathrm{KL}(q_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\Vert g_{\boldsymbol{\beta}})$. The coefficient update is then the same as at $w_S=1$, and only the loadings see survival at weight $w_S$. The weight is chosen for each dataset from $\{1,2,5,10,20,50\}$ by five-fold cross-validated partial log-likelihood [@Verweij1993], with ties going to the smaller weight. A second variant replaces the factorized posterior for $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ with a joint Gaussian. Both were evaluated in simulation (@sec-res-sim). The same rule was applied to the PDAC training data, with nested cross-validation to estimate the concordance of the whole procedure (@sec-res-cv).

We will compare this rule with two alternatives for choosing the weight. The first calibrates the power on the partial likelihood. SafeBayes chooses the power that minimizes a sequential predictive loss [@Grunwald2017], and Holmes and Walker match the expected information in the power posterior to that of a correctly specified model [@HolmesWalker2017]. The second divides each loss by a normalizing constant and mixes them with one parameter, as DeSurv does for its reconstruction and Cox losses [@Young2026]. Expressed in the units of our objective, this rule sets the relative survival weight and also rescales the KL terms. Each candidate will be compared with the cross-validated weight on the simulation grid of @sec-sim-design and in training cross-validation. The comparison will look at how often the planted program is recovered relative to the matched two-step fit, the calibration slope of validation survival on the risk score (@sec-data), whether the fits converge, and how much programs that match no planted program contribute to the risk score. On the real data, a weight that lets survival change the loadings is useful only if it keeps cross-validated concordance close to that at $w_S=1$.

## Prediction in New Cohorts {#sec-prediction}

The survival weight, the gene set, the input scaling and the rank were chosen by training cross-validation (@sec-tuning and @sec-rank). Validation cohorts are log-transformed once where needed, standardized within their own cohort and restricted to the training genes. Genes missing from a cohort are set to zero after standardization within that cohort, so they add nothing to the projection. The risk score is $\boldsymbol{\eta} = \mathbf{Y}_{\text{new}}E[\mathbf{F}]E[\boldsymbol{\beta}]$ with the loadings and coefficients frozen at their training values, and its direction is fixed by the training fit before any validation outcome is seen.

## Simulation Studies {#sec-sim-design}

We ran three simulation studies (Table \ref{tab:sim-design}). All use the same generator: three true programs, the third of which is prognostic and carries a small, set share of the expression variance, with Weibull survival times and about 30% censoring. Every fit starts from rank seven. The first study (the fixed-weight simulation) asks whether the survival-weighted fit recovers the planted program at 50 and 2,000 genes across a wide grid of fixed weights. The second (the cross-validated-weight simulation) chooses the weight by cross-validation and compares the result with the matched two-step fit, and also runs permuted-survival null datasets. The third (the near-threshold simulation) lowers the planted share toward the detection threshold, where an unsupervised factorization starts to miss the program, and compares strong survival with a weaker, realistic survival signal.

## PDAC Data and Evaluation {#sec-data}

The model is trained on TCGA-PAAD (144 patients) and CPTAC (129) [@Raphael2017; @Cao2021], with 139 deaths among the 273 patients. The five held-out cohorts contain 616 records from 568 donors. They are Dijk [@Dijk2020], Moffitt GEO array [@Moffitt2015], PACA-AU array and PACA-AU RNA-seq [@Bailey2016], and Puleo array [@Puleo2018]. Every RNA-seq cohort is log-transformed once. Expression is standardized within each cohort. Genes are selected with a procedure adapted from @Young2026. In each training cohort, genes are ranked by expression mean and by variance, and the 3,000 genes with the smallest sum of the two ranks are kept. Intersecting the two cohorts' sets leaves 2,218 genes. No survival screen is applied. The working model has rank $K=5$ without pruning, chosen by training cross-validation (@sec-rank). Some results were computed for an earlier fit at rank 7, before the rank was chosen, and are labeled with that rank.

The model is fitted to the 273 training patients pooled, after expression is standardized within each cohort. The pooled fit has one baseline hazard and no cohort strata. A version that stratifies the baseline hazard by cohort is implemented but has not yet been evaluated on these data. External discrimination is Harrell's concordance [@Harrell1982] with percentile bootstrap intervals [@EfronTibshirani1993]. Differences between the supervised and two-step fits use a paired bootstrap within each cohort (2,000 replicates), pooled across cohorts by equally weighting the series-specific differences. A donor bootstrap keeps records from the same donor together while preserving the within-series concordance comparisons. Calibration is the slope of a Cox model of validation survival on the risk score. A slope of 1 means the training coefficients predict hazard differences of the observed size, a slope below 1 means they overstate them, and a slope above 1 means they shrink them toward zero. The PACA-AU array and RNA-seq series share 47 donors, and the RNA-seq series contains a repeated donor. We also report the pooled difference after excluding that series.

## Tuning Protocol {#sec-tuning}

From now on, every modeling choice, from preprocessing and gene screening to the priors, the rank, the survival weight and the tuning of comparators, is made by simulation and by five-fold cross-validation on the 273 training patients. The folds are balanced by cohort and event status, so every training fold contains both cohorts. No part of the training data is held out as a separate test set. In training cross-validation at rank 7 the concordance had a standard error of 0.024 across five folds, so one fold of about 55 patients estimates concordance with a standard deviation near 0.05. A 20% hold-out would therefore be too noisy to separate settings whose concordance differs by 0.01 or less, and it would remove a fifth of the patients from every fit. A paired comparison counts as close when the difference is within one standard error of the paired fold differences. In that case five-fold cross-validation is repeated with four more random partitions of the patients into folds. The five validation series and the matched methylation validation set only score a model that is already fixed. Their results are reported, but they are never used to choose between models or settings. DeSurv used the same protocol on the same training and validation cohorts: it chose every hyperparameter by five-fold cross-validation in the training data and scored the validation cohorts once with the final model, apart from sensitivity analyses reported after selection [@Young2026].

At rank 7, training cross-validation chose the survival weight, the number of genes (from 2,218 to all 17,900 genes shared by the two cohorts) and whether to screen genes for a survival association inside each fold. It also compared the gene screen, the input scaling and the rank with alternatives (@sec-rank). The validation series were scored once after the fit was fixed. The DeSurv comparator used its published settings rather than a new search on our folds (@sec-comparators).

## Gene Screen, Input Scaling and Rank {#sec-rank}

The gene screen and the input scaling were compared with alternatives by five-fold training cross-validation, using concordance within cohort. The alternative is a different preprocessing configuration, not only a different ranking rule: it z-scores each cohort, quantile-normalizes the merged matrix and keeps the 2,000 genes of largest variance. Neither screen uses outcomes, so each was computed once on all training patients, as in DeSurv. The alternative scalings were division by the within-cohort standard deviation, with the Cox projection centered, and the within-patient rank transform used by DeSurv followed by z-scores within cohort [@Young2026]. We kept the current choice unless an alternative improved concordance by more than one standard error of the paired fold difference.

The rank is not chosen by pruning. In simulation, unpruned fits recovered the planted program in 17 of 20 and 19 of 20 datasets across two noise levels, while ordinary and protected ELBO pruning each recovered 2 of 20 at both levels and retained median ranks of two and one. We chose the rank by five-fold training cross-validation with the one-standard-error rule: the smallest $K$ from 2 to 12 whose mean concordance is within one standard error of the best. Without pruning the fit keeps every column it starts with, so cross-validation chooses the fitted rank. The number of programs with nonzero loadings is whatever the empirical Bayes priors leave active at that rank, and we report it with the number of survival-active programs.

## Sensitivity to the Priors {#sec-model-checks}

Sensitivity analyses refit the model with alternatives to the priors of @sec-model, using the simulation cells of @sec-sim-design and the five training folds, and compare recovery, false-active programs, convergence, calibration and cross-validated concordance. For the scores and loadings, the alternative is a point-exponential prior, a mixture of a point mass at zero and an exponential distribution, fitted to expression divided by its within-cohort standard deviation without centering. This gives a nonnegative factorization like DeSurv's, in which each program is an additive set of genes. Because that input keeps each cohort's mean level, the training comparison counts only pairs of patients from the same cohort. For the coefficients, the alternatives are point-Laplace and point-normal priors, which can set a coefficient exactly to zero, and the point-normal prior also gives a posterior probability that each coefficient is nonzero. The comparison rests on recovery of the planted program, convergence and cross-validated concordance. Survival-active programs that match no planted program are reported with the size of their coefficients, since a program with a small coefficient changes the risk score little. The comparisons are reported in Appendices \ref{app:lf-prior} and \ref{app:beta-prior}. A changed model would be scored once in the validation series after it is fixed.

## Proposed Extension to Several Data Types {#sec-mmodal}

The single-modality model is the case $M=1$ of a model for $M$ matched data types with shared patient scores and modality-specific loadings:
$$
\mathbf{Y}_m = \mathbf{L}\mathbf{F}_m^\top + \mathbf{E}_m,\qquad E_{m,ij}\sim N(0,\tau_{mj}^{-1}),\qquad \eta_i=\sum_k z_{ik}\beta_k,\qquad \mathbf{Z}=\sum_{m=1}^M \mathbf{Y}_m\mathbf{F}_m .
$$
Each program has a separate point-Laplace prior $g_{\mathbf{f}_{mk}}$ for each modality. Estimating the priors by empirical Bayes allows a sparser prior for the much larger set of methylation sites. Every update keeps the single-modality form. The score update sums the expression terms over modalities, each $\mathbf{F}_m$ update uses the joint score, and the coefficient update uses the joint score with its variance summed over modalities. With $M=1$ every formula reduces to the one above.

The derivation identifies a balance problem the single-modality model does not have. The precision of the shared scores sums over all features, so the modality with more features, methylation in the planned application, would dominate $\mathbf{L}$, and the survival share falls with the total number of features. Modality-specific weights on the reconstruction terms may therefore be needed. They will be derived and checked in simulation before any real-data fit.

Before the joint fit, we fitted the single-modality model at rank 5 to methylation alone on the 144 TCGA patients with matched expression, methylation and survival (75 deaths). Methylation at each CpG site is measured as the methylated fraction, between 0 and 1. Sites whose mean fraction on these patients lies between 0.1 and 0.9 are eligible, which removes sites that are almost always methylated or almost always unmethylated and leaves 182,934. These are ranked by variance, and the model was fitted to the top 10,000, 25,000, 50,000 and 100,000 sites and to all eligible sites, under both prior setups of @sec-model-checks with a Normal coefficient prior. Neither screen uses outcomes, and both were computed, with imputation of missing values, before the patients were split into folds. The comparator is the expression fit on the same patients and five folds. A methylation program counts as not seen in expression when its patient scores correlate below 0.5 in absolute value with every expression program and it is survival-active in the full fit and in at least three of the five training folds. We also compared the two sets of patient program scores by canonical correlation and by regressing each methylation program on all expression programs. With 144 patients the cross-validated concordance is noisy, so this comparison is descriptive. Cross-validation was run only for the numbers of sites at which the full fit converged. Methylation programs with survival signal that expression lacks would motivate the joint model. If there are none, the case for the joint model rests on interpretation.

We will implement the model in one fitter and check that its $M=1$ case reproduces the single-modality fit: the posterior means of the scores, loadings and coefficients and the final ELBO must agree to a relative tolerance of $10^{-6}$ on two test datasets, one of them with cohort strata. We will evaluate the extension in two-modality simulations with modality-specific programs and one shared prognostic program. These simulations will show how often the joint fit recovers the shared program and whether it converges. The simulations will also show whether methylation, with many more features, dominates the shared scores. The planned application fits expression alone, methylation alone and both on the matched TCGA patients with the same five folds, with validation in ICGC PACA-AU. The fixed joint and expression-only fits will be scored once in the ICGC set. We will also assess whether adding methylation identifies a prognostic program missed by the expression-only fit.

<!-- RESULT (one fitter for M data types): M = 1 agreement (largest relative difference), KL helper check, two-modality simulation recovery / false-active / convergence, descriptive real-data CV C for expression, methylation and both. -->

## Comparators, Risk Groups and Program Classification {#sec-comparators}

Every comparator was trained on the same 273 training patients, and each score's direction was fixed on the training data. DeSurv used the authors' software, preprocessing and reported settings (rank 3), which the authors selected on the same two training cohorts [@Young2026]. An elastic-net Cox model on the 2,218 genes [@Simon2011] chose its mixing and penalty parameters by cross-validation on the training folds. PurIST [@Rashid2020] entered as a Cox model on its basal-like probability. A clinical model was planned, but no stage, grade, age or margin field is recorded in both training cohorts and all five validation series, so it was not fitted. Unsupervised EBMF at ranks 7, 15 and 40 followed by Cox regression tested whether a larger unsupervised rank would close any gap. Pooled hazard ratios are per SD of each score from Cox models stratified by series, with robust intervals clustered on donor.

For risk groups, one cutpoint per score maximized the log-rank statistic on the out-of-fold training scores, with at least 20% of patients in each group, and was applied unchanged in every validation series. A program was called a main prognostic program when its standardized coefficient was at least 0.25 of the largest, its signed share of the risk-score variance, $\mathrm{Cov}(\eta_k,\eta)/\mathrm{Var}(\eta)$, was at least 5%, and it was survival-active in at least four of the five training folds after matching loadings with absolute correlation at least 0.7.

We compared the projection score with the $\boldsymbol{\eta}=\mathbf{L}\boldsymbol{\beta}$ parameterization at rank 5. In that model the risk score uses each patient's latent program scores, estimated from all programs at once, and a new patient's scores are estimated by fold-in under the frozen priors. Because $\mathbf{Y}\approx\mathbf{L}\mathbf{F}^\top$, the projection score satisfies $\mathbf{Y}\mathbf{F}\approx\mathbf{L}(\mathbf{F}^\top\mathbf{F})$ up to noise. It mixes the latent scores through the overlap between programs, and the two scores agree, up to scale, when the loadings are orthogonal, for example when the programs share no genes. Both models got the same input matrix, priors, starting values, rank and folds, so only the parameterization of the hazard differs. Held-out training folds are scored by fold-in for the latent-score model and by projection for ours, the same contrast as in an external cohort. We compared recovery, survival-active programs that match no planted program, convergence and validation concordance in simulation at $w_S=1$ and 10, cross-validated concordance on the training data, the genes of the fitted programs, the correlation between the two risk scores, and concordance in the validation series.

# Results {#sec-results}

## Survival Weight in Simulation {#sec-res-sim}

With 2,000 genes and $w_S=1$, the survival-weighted fit recovered the planted program in 10 of 10 datasets in each of the three variance cells, with a mean of 0.9, 0.1 and 0.0 false-active programs, and every fit converged (Figure \ref{fig:sim-s9}). Five-fold training cross-validation chose $w_S=1$ in 55 of 60 datasets. The other choices were the weight targeting a survival precision share of 0.2 in three datasets and $w_S=10$ in two. Every fit with $w_S\ge40$ stopped at 300 sweeps without converging, and recovery fell in most cells. With 50 genes, all fixed positive weights recovered the program, and false activity rose with weight. The share-targeted arm did not recover the program. The cause of non-convergence at large weights has not been found. In those fits the largest $|E\beta_k|$ ranged from 17 to 26. The SD of the true predictor ranged from 9 to 26.

At 2,000 genes, the fitted risks at $w_S=1$ were attenuated. The median validation calibration slope was 1.45, 2.16 and 3.23 across the three variance cells, against about 1 for the true predictor. A slope above 1 means that the fitted risks are shrunk toward zero. Validation concordance ranged from 0.94 to 0.99. The survival share of the planted program's loading precision explains part of this. At $w_S=1$ it fell from 0.79–1.00 with 50 genes to 0.01–0.20 with 2,000.

\caption[Survival-weighted fit with 2,000 genes against the survival weight $w_S$ (the fixed-weight simulation)]{Survival-weighted fit with 2,000 genes against the survival weight $w_S$ (the fixed-weight simulation): recovery of the planted program, mean number of false-active programs, median exact-time validation calibration slope, converged fits, median survival share of matched loading precision and mean validation concordance. Curves are grouped by the planted program's share of expression variance. Ten datasets per cell.}\label{fig:sim-s9}
\end{figure}
```

The matched two-step fit uses the $w_S=0$ loadings and also recovers the planted program in 10 of 10 datasets in every one of these cells (Table \ref{tab:strength}). The supervised fits at $w_S=1$ converged with few false-active programs.

When the weight was chosen for each dataset by cross-validated partial log-likelihood (Figure \ref{fig:sim-s13}), the chosen weight grew with the strength of the planted program: 1 or 2 in the weakest cells, 5 at 1% variance and 10 at 5%. The rule never chose 20 or 50, the weights at which fits stopped converging. At the chosen weight, recovery equalled the two-step fit's in every cell. Validation concordance was equal in the two stronger cells and higher by 0.003 to 0.007 in the two weakest, and false activity was lower than the two-step fit's in the stronger cells. The coefficients stayed attenuated, with median slopes of 1.24 to 1.45 in the three strong-survival cells, compared with 0.96 to 1.16 for two-step. Under permuted survival the block-weight variant averaged 1.1 false-active programs at its most often chosen weight. The joint posterior for $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ gave the same recoveries and concordance as the factorized one, to within 0.004.

Supervision changed discovery only near the detection threshold (Figure \ref{fig:sim-s14}). With strong survival and a planted share of 0.05% of the expression variance, the supervised fit at $w_S=1$ recovered the program in 5 of 10 datasets. The two-step fit recovered none. Mean validation concordance was 0.156 higher in the supervised fit. The supervised fit had the higher concordance in 29 of the 30 strong-survival datasets, and the gain shrank as the program became easier to find, to 0.041 at a share of 0.1% and 0.008 at 0.2%. Both fits averaged more than two false-active programs in the hardest cell, and their contribution to the risk score is examined below. With realistic survival, where the true predictor gives a validation concordance of about 0.74, the gains were small: 0.038 at a share of 0.05%, where no fit recovered the program, and 0.002 to 0.008 at the larger shares. A fixed $w_S=5$ recovered the planted program in more datasets with strong survival and fewer datasets with realistic survival. Its calibration slopes ranged from 0.04 to 0.65. This contrast motivates choosing the weight from the data.

Points show individual datasets and diamonds show cell means for the paired differences. Ten datasets per cell.}\label{fig:sim-s14}
\end{figure}

We also examined the combined contribution of the nonmatched programs, including those below the activity threshold. In the near-threshold simulation cells with planted shares of 0.1% and 0.2%, the median ratio of nonmatched to total risk-score variance reached 1.3% at $w_S=1$. Removing the nonmatched programs changed mean concordance by at most 0.008 across the supervised and two-step arms in these cells. At 0.05% planted share the median ratios ranged from 8.7% to 68.8%. With strong survival they were 8.7% for the supervised fit and 68.8% for two-step. These post hoc comparisons describe predictive contributions, separate from the count of false-active programs. In a simulation that planted one strong and one near-threshold prognostic program together, the supervised fit at $w_S=1$ and the two-step fit each recovered the near-threshold program in 9 of 10 datasets, while a fixed $w_S=5$ recovered it in 2.

The planned evaluation will compare the alternative weights of @sec-choose-weight on the same grid and add cells with more realistic survival effects.


## Training Cross-Validation on PDAC {#sec-res-cv}

At rank 5, the working model had a mean within-cohort cross-validated concordance of 0.655 (SE 0.029), with every fold fit converged, and Programs 2, 4 and 5 were survival-active in the fit to all training patients (@sec-res-programs). Against the two-step fit on the same folds, the supervised fit had a mean fold concordance of 0.660 (SE 0.027), against 0.656 (SE 0.029), a paired difference of 0.004 (SE 0.004) (Table \ref{tab:training-cv}). Every fold fit converged in both arms, and three programs were survival-active in each fit to all patients.

Survival did not change the loadings. Its share of the loading precision was $3\times10^{-7}$ to $1.2\times10^{-6}$, against 0.01 to 0.2 in the 2,000-gene simulation, and the supervised and unsupervised loadings agreed at $|r|=1.000$ for every program. Two features of the real data combine to make the share this small. The real coefficients are small, at most 0.42 per standard deviation of the score in any fold, and the share scales with $E[\beta_k^2]$. The real programs are also high-variance programs with a large expression precision, whereas the simulated program carried 0.25% to 5% of the variance. The small concordance difference therefore comes from the joint coefficient update with its Normal shrinkage prior.

Concordance changed little with the number of genes (Figure \ref{fig:size-curve}). Both arms were level from 2,218 to 8,001 genes, between 0.655 and 0.664, and about 0.025 lower at 12,001 and 17,900 genes, and every size was within about one standard error of the others. Screening genes for a univariate survival association inside each fold gave gains of 0.008 to 0.023 over an outcome-free set of the same size, each within about 1.5 paired standard errors, and no screened set beat the full 2,218-gene fit. On permuted-survival datasets the fit at $w_S=1$ produced 0.1 to 0.5 false-active programs per cell.

At rank 7, a refit that chose the weight by training cross-validated partial log-likelihood on these patients, over weights from 1 to 50, selected $w_S=1$. The curve was flat. The cross-validated partial log-likelihood changed from $-775.168$ at weight one to $-775.429$ at weight 50. Nested cross-validation gave $C=0.656$ (SE 0.027), compared with 0.663 at the fixed weight. At weight 50, survival supplied a median of $7.3\times10^{-5}$ of the loading precision for active programs, and the loadings still agreed with those of the unsupervised fit to the reported precision. The model therefore keeps $w_S=1$.

Training cross-validation also supported the gene screen and the input scaling (Table \ref{tab:inputs-rank}). In concordance within cohort at rank 7, the alternative preprocessing was lower by 0.012 (paired SE 0.014), division by the within-cohort standard deviation by 0.020 (SE 0.007) and the rank transform by 0.017 (SE 0.009). Across ranks, concordance was flat from $K=5$ to 12, between 0.649 and 0.666, and lower from $K=2$ to 4, between 0.611 and 0.620. The one-standard-error rule selected $K=5$. Its concordance was 0.003 below that of $K=7$ (paired SE 0.007), all five of its fold fits converged against three at $K=7$, and three programs were survival-active in the full fit at every rank from 5 to 8. Every column kept nonzero loadings at every rank, so the priors did not remove programs. The rule picks the smallest rank on the plateau and does not show that $K=5$ predicts better than $K=7$. Because these comparisons are close, we repeated the five-fold cross-validation with four more random partitions of the patients. Averaged over the five partitions, the one-standard-error rule again selected $K=5$, with concordance 0.643 against a best of 0.651 at $K=12$. Four of the five partitions selected $K=5$ on their own and one selected $K=10$. $K=5$ converged in all 25 fold fits, against 18 at $K=7$. The alternative preprocessing was 0.002 lower on average (SE 0.008), so the gene screen also stays. The working model therefore uses $K=5$. Its five programs match Programs 1 to 5 of the rank-7 fit, with score correlations of 0.92 to 0.995, and the two rank-7 programs it drops were not survival-active. Programs 2 and 5 are survival-active at both ranks. Programs 3 and 4 lie near the 1.96 threshold: Program 3 falls below it at $K=5$ ($z$ from 3.0 to 1.5) and Program 4 rises above it ($z$ from 1.9 to 2.4).

No alternative prior improved on the point-Laplace and Normal priors. A point-exponential prior on the scores and loadings, fitted to nonnegative input, lowered within-cohort cross-validated concordance at rank 7 from 0.658 to between 0.573 and 0.635 across four input setups, and at most one of five folds converged. At rank 5 it gave 0.519 against 0.655. Shared point-Laplace, point-normal and Normal coefficient priors gave within-cohort concordance of 0.649 to 0.656 at rank 7, against 0.658 for the Normal prior, with nearly the same simulation results, and 0.648 to 0.649 at rank 5, against 0.655. The working model therefore keeps them. Appendices \ref{app:lf-prior} and \ref{app:beta-prior} give the comparisons.

## External Validation {#sec-res-external}

At rank 5, the working model's concordance in the five held-out cohorts was 0.599 in Dijk, 0.538 in Moffitt, 0.664 in PACA-AU array, 0.704 in PACA-AU RNA-seq and 0.645 in Puleo (Table \ref{tab:external}, Figure \ref{fig:external}). The equal-weight mean over the series was 0.630 (95% donor-bootstrap interval 0.587 to 0.670), and the mean weighted by the number of comparable patient pairs was 0.628 (0.596 to 0.662). Genes absent from a series were set to zero after standardization within that series. The two-step fit scored nearly the same. The equal-weight pooled difference was $-0.001$ (95% record-bootstrap interval $-0.009$ to 0.007, donor-bootstrap interval $-0.010$ to 0.008), and $-0.002$ ($-0.011$ to 0.007) without PACA-AU RNA-seq. A Cox model stratified by cohort gave a hazard ratio of 1.39 (1.26 to 1.53) per standard deviation of the supervised risk score, and 1.40 (1.27 to 1.54) for the two-step score. With robust intervals clustered on donor these become 1.24 to 1.56 and 1.24 to 1.57. DeSurv refitted on the same training patients gave 1.43 (1.25 to 1.64), against 1.50 (1.31 to 1.72) in the original analysis [@Young2026].

## Comparison With Other Prognostic Models {#sec-res-comparators}

The working model's mean concordance over the five series was 0.630, against 0.614 for DeSurv and 0.619 for elastic-net Cox trained on the same patients (Table \ref{tab:comparators}). The paired differences were 0.016 ($-0.009$ to 0.043) against DeSurv, 0.011 ($-0.008$ to 0.031) against elastic-net Cox, 0.031 ($-0.004$ to 0.066) against PurIST and $-0.001$ ($-0.010$ to 0.008) against the two-step fit, and each interval included zero. The elastic-net model selected the ridge penalty. PurIST alone had a mean concordance of 0.599. EBMF followed by Cox regression did worse at ranks 15 and 40 than at rank 5, with differences of 0.055 and 0.049 whose intervals excluded zero, and calibration slopes of 0.10 to 0.49 that show the unpenalized Cox step overfitting with 139 training deaths.

The training cutpoint was 0.618 SD for the supervised score and 0.485 SD for the two-step score. Applied unchanged in the validation series, it gave pooled high-versus-low hazard ratios of 1.69 (1.34 to 2.14) and 1.78 (1.43 to 2.23), with 128 and 147 of the 616 validation records in the high-risk group. In every series the supervised high-risk group held a larger proportion of basal-like tumours by PurIST (0.31 to 0.73, against 0.02 to 0.10 in the low-risk group) and of permissive CAF (permCAF) tumours by DeCAF (0.77 to 1.00, against 0.39 to 0.72). The supervised score's pooled hazard ratio per training SD was 1.54 unadjusted, 1.53 after adjusting for PurIST subtype and 1.44 after adjusting for DeCAF subtype.

## Latent-Score and Projection Parameterizations {#sec-res-lb}

The two parameterizations gave nearly the same model on the training data. At rank 5 the latent-score model had a mean within-cohort cross-validated concordance of 0.652 and the projection model 0.655, a paired difference of 0.003 (SE 0.004). Every fold fit converged in both. The two fitted risk scores correlated 0.998, and each pair of corresponding programs had the same 20 genes with the largest loadings. The same three programs were survival-active in both. In the validation series the two models had pair-weighted mean concordance of 0.627 and 0.628, a difference of 0.001 (95% donor-bootstrap interval $-0.002$ to 0.005).

In simulation, recovery was similar except near the detection threshold. At $w_S=1$ both recovered the planted program in every dataset of the three variance cells of the fixed-weight study, and near the detection threshold the latent-score model recovered it in 5 of 10 datasets and the projection model in 4. At $w_S=1$ the latent-score model marked more programs survival-active that matched no planted program, a mean of 1.2 to 1.8 per fit in the three variance cells against 0.0 to 0.9 for the projection model. At $w_S=10$ both marked few such programs, and near the detection threshold the latent-score model recovered the planted program in 7 of 10 datasets and the projection model in 3. The simulation run reported numerical warnings whose messages were not saved, which limits what these runs show about numerical stability.

We keep the projection model. It predicts as well as the latent-score model, in the three variance cells it produced fewer survival-active programs without a planted match at the survival weight used on the real data, though near the detection threshold it produced more (2.9 per fit against 1.4), and it scores a new patient directly from measured expression without fold-in. The two models also differ in what a coefficient means. In the latent-score model, $\exp(\beta_k)$ is the hazard ratio per unit of latent program activity, given the other programs. In the projection model it is the hazard ratio per standard deviation of the projection score, a weighted sum of gene levels. Because $\mathbf{Y}\mathbf{F}\approx\mathbf{L}(\mathbf{F}^\top\mathbf{F})$, the projection mixes the latent activities of programs that share genes. On these data the two were nearly equal, with correlations of 0.985 to 0.999 between each latent score and its projection.

## Programs {#sec-res-programs}

In the working model three programs were survival-active. Program 2 was protective at its positive pole ($E[\beta]=-0.372$), while the positive poles of Programs 4 and 5 were adverse (0.209 and 0.230). Table \ref{tab:programs} gives the coefficient estimates and the genes at both poles. Program 3 had a positive coefficient (0.101) below the activity threshold, and Program 1 a coefficient of zero. Only Program 2 was classified as a main prognostic program (Table \ref{tab:program-rule}). Programs 4 and 5 met the coefficient and variance thresholds but were survival-active in only three and two of the five training folds. Survival supplied at most $2.5\times10^{-6}$ of any program's loading precision, so no program is survival-dominated. In saved simulation fits the coefficient and variance parts of the rule kept the planted program in all 80 cross-validated-weight fits and rejected 35 of 36 false-active directions, but rejected only 61 of 128 in the two-step near-threshold fits. The fold-stability part was not checked in simulation.

At the protective pole of Program 2, the largest loadings included genes associated with exocrine and classical epithelial expression, and its adverse pole included \textit{LDHA}, \textit{PGK1} and \textit{SLC16A3}. Program 4 has acinar enzyme genes at its adverse pole and B-cell and interferon genes at its other pole. Acinar content in a bulk tumor sample often reflects normal pancreas in the sample, so its label describes the genes rather than tumor biology. Program 5 showed mitotic and stromal or immune signatures, with a less specific subtype interpretation (Table \ref{tab:enrichment}).

The rank-5 programs correspond one to one with Programs 1 to 5 of a fit at rank 7, with score correlations of 0.92 to 0.995 and 14 to 23 of the 25 largest loadings shared at each pole. The two extra rank-7 programs, one of them myeloid, were not survival-active. Programs 2 and 5 were survival-active at both ranks, while Program 3 was active only at rank 7 and Program 4 only at rank 5.

Separate external Cox regressions estimated protective associations for Program 2 and adverse associations for Program 4 in all five series, and adverse associations for Program 5 in two (Table \ref{tab:external-program-direction}). These regressions are unadjusted, so their directions need not agree with the coefficients from the joint training fit. The corresponding Kaplan--Meier curves (Figures \ref{fig:km-program-2} to \ref{fig:km-program-5}) group patients by the training coefficient's risk direction. Cohort-specific coefficient fits in TCGA-PAAD and CPTAC remain part of the planned evaluation.

Signature scores provide another comparison with published PDAC subtypes and stromal signatures. We averaged the available standardized genes in each published signature within each cohort and correlated those scores with fixed program scores. Program 2 correlated negatively with the Moffitt basal-like signature in pooled training data ($\rho=-0.68$) and across external series ($-0.74$ to $-0.69$). Program 4 correlated with the Bailey ADEX signature ($\rho=0.73$ in training, 0.50 to 0.77 externally) and the Collisson exocrine-like signature (0.73, 0.47 to 0.75), and negatively with the Bailey immunogenic signature ($-0.29$, $-0.63$ to $-0.12$). Program 5's correlations with the DeSurv stromal-immune signature were weak ($\rho=0.18$ in training, $-0.08$ to 0.14 externally), so its enrichment gives limited evidence of a reproducible stromal association. Across the external series, correlations with the saved PurIST basal-like probabilities were $-0.66$ to $-0.45$ for Program 2, 0.05 to 0.50 for Program 4 and $-0.20$ to 0.00 for Program 5.

## Methylation Alone {#sec-res-meth}

Methylation alone predicted survival less well than expression on the same 144 patients. With point-Laplace priors, mean cross-validated concordance was 0.50 to 0.55 across the five numbers of CpG sites, against 0.582 for expression on the same folds, with paired differences of $-0.037$ to $-0.080$ (standard errors 0.033 to 0.045). With point-exponential priors, the full fits at 10,000 to 50,000 sites did not converge within 300 sweeps, so only 100,000 and all sites were cross-validated, giving 0.539 and 0.512 against 0.620 for expression. Methylation was lower in all seven comparisons. All expression fits converged once they were allowed up to 1,000 sweeps. Every full fit kept five programs with nonzero loadings, and no methylation program was survival-active in the full fit and in at least three of the five folds while correlating below 0.5 with every expression program.

The two data types share their strongest variation but not all of it. Across the seven methylation fits, the first two canonical correlations between the methylation and expression program scores were 0.90 to 0.92 and 0.85 to 0.88, and the fifth was 0.00 to 0.17. Some methylation programs recurred across numbers of sites while correlating below 0.5 with every expression program. The clearest, a point-Laplace program at 100,000 and all sites, was almost unexplained by the five expression programs together ($R^2$ of 0.06 and 0.04), and its strongest gene-set associations were allograft rejection and TNF-$\alpha$ signaling, which suggests an immune component. The methylation program most related to tumor purity correlated up to 0.87 with ABSOLUTE purity estimates and overlapped the first expression program. Among 9,086 pairs of a promoter CpG and one of the 2,218 genes, 76.5% had a negative correlation between methylation and expression, as expected for promoter methylation, though these correlations are not adjusted for purity. The fixed methylation fits have not been scored in the ICGC set. These results are descriptive at $n=144$, and they leave open how many CpG sites a joint fit should use: prediction was best at 10,000 sites, while the methylation programs that expression does not explain appeared only at 100,000 sites and above.

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

## Loading and Coefficient Estimates

On the PDAC data the supervised and two-step fits gave the same loadings and nearly the same predictions, in training cross-validation and in the validation series. The joint fit propagates posterior loading uncertainty and shrinks the coefficients, but at the survival weight chosen from the data, survival supplied almost none of the loading precision. These results therefore do not show improved molecular program discovery on these data.

The simulations show where supervised discovery can help and how far the current model gets there. A small survival weight acts mostly on low-variance programs, since the survival share grows as a program's variance share falls. Near the detection threshold the supervised fit found programs the two-step fit missed and predicted much better when survival was strong. When the planted program was easy to find, or survival was as weak as on the real data, the two fits were nearly the same. A larger fixed weight moved the loadings in strong-survival settings but overfit in realistic ones and failed to converge with 2,000 genes. Choosing the weight by cross-validated partial log-likelihood avoided those weights and adapted to the signal, but it left the coefficients attenuated in the strong-survival cells. That combination makes a data-driven weight the main open problem of the project.

Placing the latent scores in the Cox model, $\boldsymbol{\eta}=\mathbf{L}\boldsymbol{\beta}$, gave nearly the same programs and predictions on these data, so the projection score costs nothing in accuracy and avoids fold-in for new patients (@sec-res-lb). Methylation alone predicted less well than expression and showed no survival-active program that expression misses, although some methylation programs are not explained by the expression programs (@sec-res-meth). The case for the joint model therefore rests on interpretation.

## Limitations

The choice of the survival weight was checked at rank 7 and has not yet been repeated at rank 5. The survival-active label of Programs 3 and 4 differs between ranks 5 and 7, so it is not stable for those two programs. Training cross-validation supports the gene screen and the input scaling. Comparisons on the five validation series had informed these choices earlier, so those series are not untouched by development. The rank and screen comparisons were repeated over five random partitions of the same 273 patients. That shows the choices do not depend on how patients are assigned to folds, but it does not measure sampling variability. The reported fit pools the two training cohorts with one baseline hazard, so it does not model a difference in baseline hazard between TCGA-PAAD and CPTAC. The donor bootstrap and the donor-clustered hazard-ratio intervals account for repeated donors while leaving the pooled estimand conditional on the observed series. DeSurv used its reported settings rather than a new search on our training folds. Some training folds stopped at the sweep limit. The simulations use a single generator, and the strongest simulated survival signals exceed those observed in the real data.

## Continuing Work

We will develop a data-driven survival weight that lets survival affect the loadings where the data support it. Candidates are the cross-validated weight already tested, a calibrated power on the partial likelihood, and normalized loss terms (@sec-choose-weight). Each will be compared in simulation and in training cross-validation on PDAC. The extension to several data types (@sec-mmodal) will start from a fitter that reproduces the current model for one modality. We will release the selected model as an R package with a single fitting function and use it to regenerate the manuscript results.

## Priors on the Scores and Loadings

\label{app:lf-prior}A point-exponential prior on $\mathbf{L}$ and $\mathbf{F}$ keeps every score and loading nonnegative, as in a nonnegative matrix factorization such as DeSurv. Tables \ref{tab:lf-prior-sim} and \ref{tab:lf-prior-real} compare it with the point-Laplace prior in simulation and in five-fold training cross-validation. The point-exponential fits need nonnegative input and a centered Cox projection, and three of the inputs remove or absorb the difference in mean expression between the two training cohorts. In simulation the point-exponential prior recovered the planted program as often as point-Laplace. Point-exponential fits also marked more programs survival-active that matched no planted program. Such programs are expected, and where their size was measured their coefficients were mostly a tenth to a quarter of the planted program's. The difference appeared on the training data, where the point-exponential prior lowered concordance by 0.023 to 0.085 under every input, and at most one of five folds converged. At the rank chosen by cross-validation, $K=5$, the point-exponential prior gave 0.519 against 0.655. Apart from that check, both comparisons in this appendix use rank 7, the rank in use before training cross-validation selected rank 5. The working model keeps the point-Laplace prior.

```

## Prior on the Survival Coefficients

\label{app:beta-prior}A sparse coefficient prior can set a program's coefficient exactly to zero, and the point-normal prior gives each program a posterior probability of a nonzero coefficient that could replace the activity threshold. Table \ref{tab:beta-prior} compares the Normal prior of the reported fit with point-Laplace and point-normal priors shared across programs, and with a shared Normal prior that separates sharing from sparsity. At rank 7 the four priors gave nearly the same fits. Concordance differed by at most 0.009, and recovery, calibration slopes and the counts of survival-active programs were nearly the same. On the training data the point-normal inclusion probabilities were 0.94 to 1.00 for all seven programs, so they did not identify the survival-active programs. At rank 5 the three shared priors gave within-cohort concordance of 0.648 to 0.649, against 0.655 for the Normal prior. The working model keeps the Normal prior.
